name: Asynchronous Programming with C++ (book techniques without usable evidence)
listed_description: Code a C++ book benchmarks or cites; see techniques. Three of its techniques are recorded in data/wave1/raw/w1-mine-ah.json (atomic counter against mutex, alignas(64) false-sharing fix, SPSC queue with cached indices).
reason: Techniques with no usable numeric comparison. (1) std::async future-handling pattern: Chapter_07/7x06-async_future_behavior.cpp carries the code (32 tasks that only sleep_for 10 ms, with discarded, in-place, reused and vector-of-futures variants) and the lead gives 334, 166 and 22 ms, but the tasks only sleep, so the ratios count how many tasks overlap because a std::async future blocks in its destructor; they do not measure the speed of any implementation and there is no recognisable baseline library. (2) Book SPSC lock-free bounded queue: Chapter_05/5x09-SPSC_lock_free_queue.cpp carries the code (prints 1000 values) with no timings in the repo or the lead; the Chapter 13 numbers belong to the cached-index variant, recorded separately. (3) Power-of-two ring-buffer index masking instead of modulo: the & (capacity_ - 1) index is in 5x09 and 13x08, but the repo has no masking-versus-modulo benchmark and the lead gives no numbers.

name: Building Low Latency Applications with C++ (book techniques without usable evidence)
listed_description: Code a C++ book benchmarks or cites; see techniques. One technique is recorded in data/wave1/raw/w1-mine-ah.json (direct-indexed std::array maps in the order book against std::unordered_map).
reason: Techniques not recorded. (1) OptLogger against Logger (25757 against 466 cycles per log() call per the lead, Chapter12/benchmarks/logger_benchmark.cpp): the baseline is the book's own Common::Logger, which pushes one queue element per character, while OptLogger copies up to 255 characters into a 256-byte string slot of a single element; no external logger (spdlog, glog, iostreams) is in the comparison. (2) OptMemPool against MemPool (343 against 44 cycles per operation): opt_mem_pool.h differs from mem_pool.h only by wrapping the per-operation ASSERT calls in #if !defined(NDEBUG), while ASSERT in macros.h is not NDEBUG-gated, so the baseline's release build still evaluates them and their message arguments build std::string temporaries (std::to_string concatenation) on every allocate and deallocate, so the gap is assertion overhead in the baseline, not pool against new/delete; the repo has no benchmark against new/delete or std::pmr. (3) MemPool design, LFQueue, asynchronous logger, TCP socket and epoll framework, pool-backed order book, CRTP order placement, branchless fill update, RDTSC macros against clock_gettime or chrono, and four more techniques in data/seeds/seeds.json: the lead gives no numbers, and the only benchmark programs found are the three in Chapter12/benchmarks (Chapter4 holds examples only).

name: C++23 STL Cookbook, 2nd ed. companion code (book techniques)
listed_description: Code a C++ book benchmarks or cites; see techniques (quick_delete swap-and-pop, std::print and std::println, map try_emplace, bw::join).
reason: No numbers anywhere reachable. The repo README is only a title and the five sources opened (Chap03/quick-delete.cpp, Chap03/insert-map.cpp, Chap03/uniform-erasure.cpp, Chap06/join.cpp, Chap01/hello.cpp) contain no timing or benchmark code. All four techniques in the lead are directional or complexity claims only: swap-and-pop deletion on an unsorted vector against std::erase or erase-remove (complexity argument, code in Chap03/quick-delete.cpp), std::print and std::println against format with cout (Chap01), try_emplace against emplace on larger payloads (Chap03/insert-map.cpp) and bw::join against the previous edition's iostream join ('about half the size', Chap06/join.cpp). The repo has 4 stars and 10 commits.
